description: Design it, Test it, Fly it.
summary: We developed SPACEBOUND, a 3D mission design game that puts players inside a space station as its newest mission designer and shows them how real space missions are planned, built and flown, by allowing them them to experience it firsthand. It directly addresses the challenge by turning the real mission lifecycle into gameplay: across four missions of rising difficulty (a wildfire-monitoring satellite, a student CubeSat, a lunar ice-hunting orbiter and a sample grab from asteroid Bennu), the players write requirements, design their spacecraft and live with real tradeoffs where every kilogram, watt and dollar counts. Before launch, the station crew puts each design through ground testing that catches weak spots, and after the flight a verification report shows exactly which requirements passed or failed, and why. Built on NASA's OSIRIS-REx, LRO and LCROSS missions, with the Moon's south pole recreated from NASA's LOLA elevation data, SPACEBOUND lets players feel real engineering problems like limited power, minutes of radio contact, and an 18.5-minute signal delay that forces a spacecraft to land itself. In online crews, every player owns a role, just like a real mission team. Its importance is simple: mission design shouldn't be a closed room for engineers. SPACEBOUND gives students the chance to design a mission, watch it fail safely, and understand why.
details:
SPACEBOUND is a 3D mission design game built in Godot. The player joins a space station as its newest mission designer and takes four missions from an idea on paper to a real flight. Instead of only watching launches, players do the work behind them: setting requirements, making design trade-offs, getting the design tested, flying it and checking whether it met its goals.

How It Works:
The player explores a station with a Mission Design Bay, crew decks and specialists to talk to. Four missions unlock in order of difficulty: a training mission to fix a wildfire-monitoring satellite, a student CubeSat, a lunar orbiter hunting for ice at the Moon's south pole, and a sample grab from asteroid Bennu. Each mission follows the real mission lifecycle: requirements → design → ground testing → flight → verification. During design, every part costs mass, power or money. Before launch, the player walks the design to specialists who find weak spots, and can fix them or fly anyway. Each flight is a hands-on mini game: tracking a CubeSat from a ground station in Kochi, braking into lunar orbit, drilling for ice in a crater built from NASA LOLA elevation data, or touching Bennu without hitting a boulder. A report then shows which requirements passed or failed, and why. After all four missions, a Mission Review Board judges the player's portfolio.

Benefits:

  • Hands-on Learning: Students learn how missions are designed by doing it, not by reading about it.
  • Systems Thinking: Teaches requirements, trade-offs, margins and testing through play.
  • Safe Failure: Players can fail a mission and learn exactly why it failed.
  • Teamwork: In online crew mode, each player gets their own role, so no one sits idle.
  • Accessible: Free to play on an ordinary Windows laptop, with no engineering background needed.

Intended Impact:
SPACEBOUND aims to make mission design understandable for school and college students, who usually only see the launch and not the years of decisions behind it. It can be used in classrooms, science clubs and outreach events to spark interest in space engineering, especially among students who don't yet see themselves as engineers.

Development Tools and Technology Stack:

  • Game Engine: Godot 4.7 (GDScript)
  • Multiplayer: Node.js + WebSockets server hosted on Render
  • Data Processing: Python, used to turn NASA LOLA elevation data into game terrain and to prepare audio
  • 3D Assets: NASA 3D Resources (spacecraft), Creepy Cat Sci-Fi Starter Kit (free, station), Tripo Astronaut 2 by Jungle Jim (CC BY 4.0)
  • Animation: Mixamo
  • Font: Rajdhani (Google Fonts)

Creativity and Innovation:
The project turns each step of mission design into something you physically do: walking your design to the test team, aiming a ground station dish, watching a requirement turn green. The missions are built around real engineering problems, such as limited power, only minutes of radio contact per pass, and the 18.5-minute signal delay that forced OSIRIS-REx to land on its own. Online crews split the work so each player is responsible for one system, just like a real mission team.

Design Considerations:

  • Accuracy: Real mission values (from OSIRIS-REx, LRO, LCROSS and CubeSat 101) are kept separate from values simplified for gameplay.
  • Performance: A Safe Graphics mode and DirectX 12 support let it run on low-power and ARM (Snapdragon) laptops.
  • Fair Roles: Each player's role changes with the number of people in the crew.
  • Responsible Content: No NASA logos or branding, and every asset licence is credited.

Use of SI:
Claude (Anthropic) helped write most of the game's code and drafts of the dialogue, all reviewed and play-tested by our team. ChatGPT (OpenAI) and Gemini (Google) were used for brainstorming and feedback. Character voices were made with Chatterbox (from recordings of adult family members, with permission) and Kokoro, and each voice file is tagged as AI-generated in its metadata. No AI image generators were used for artwork. The only exception is the astronaut model's textures, which were edited with AI help. All SI use is also listed in the game's credits.

In essence, SPACEBOUND is more than a game about space. It is a way for any student to design a mission, watch it succeed or fail, and understand why.
